news.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
paras: On ice James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits Radiation and collisions reshape the planetary building materials. A ground-based telescope's view of Beta Pictoris. A ground-based telescope's view of Beta Pictoris.

It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

news.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
paras: Wine and roses Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business Healthy soils, native plants, and fewer chemicals are helping vineyards adapt. This vineyard, seen through an electric fence, relies on cover crops in South Africa’s Western Cape region.

The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases.

paras: Grounded FAA orders third nationwide ground stop in its history Rare nationwide ground stop could go on for awhile as FAA troubleshoots. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. “This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights,” Mullin said .

news.title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
paras: Real-world use Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed Cost and access barriers are pushing people to modified use and unapproved versions. Woman using an obesity drug injection pen.

The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy.

news.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 236 — Alienspotting
paras: When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms.

But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. paras: The company may still try to snag Starship's upper stage tomorrow (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch.

news.title: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged t
paras: Add as preferred source Curator Fraser Hunter examines the bronze leg. Duncan McGlynn In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region.

For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops.
